orientation.title: Learning on your terms
content: Welcome to Fleshsesh Academy. This course is for adults aged 18 and over who want clear information about bodies, sex, relationships and choice. You do not need a partner, previous experience, a particular identity or an intention to be sexually active. You are welcome to use the material simply to understand yourself and other people better.

You decide how much to engage with each topic. Read the topic note, choose an available format and pause whenever you want. All activities can use a fictional example. You never need to share a sexual history, trauma, health condition, photograph or private relationship detail to pass. You can skip reflective questions and use the equivalent knowledge task.

The course uses precise anatomical language where it helps explain health. People use different words for their bodies; respect their preferences in conversation. Identity does not tell you which organs someone has, which activities they enjoy, whether they can become pregnant or how they want to be treated.

Every lesson contains a short teaching text, a decision scenario, a private exercise and two questions with feedback. There is no time limit. An incorrect answer is an opportunity to revisit the explanation. Completion records understanding of the material and does not certify anyone as a safe partner or qualified practitioner.

Keep your own privacy in mind. Only write information you are comfortable keeping on the device you are using. A downloaded workbook can be opened by anyone with access to that file. A quick-exit button can move away from a page but cannot erase history, downloads or monitoring software. Use fictional examples whenever that is more comfortable.

Sexual health and consent information can bring up feelings or questions. You can stop, choose a different topic, contact an appropriate professional or speak to a support service. This curriculum offers education and ways to find help. It does not provide individual diagnosis, emergency monitoring or a legal opinion about a specific event.

Start with a learning goal that you control: ask a clearer question, understand a body term, make a boundary easier to express or identify a trusted source. You do not have to become more sexually active or adventurous. A clearer no can be as useful an outcome as a clearer yes.
orientation.activity: Choose a fictional learner and one goal from the list above. Find the consent module, the glossary and a support route. Practise pausing or choosing a text format. You can keep the goal private.

modules.title: Consent and autonomy
modules.summary: Build an active, accessible and ongoing consent practice that protects every adult's freedom to choose.

lessons.title: Consent is an active choice
objectives: Explain the Academy's standard of freely chosen, informed, specific and ongoing consent.
Distinguish an invitation from an entitlement to a particular answer.
Recognise that relationship status, appearance and previous agreement do not establish present consent.
lessons.content:
Sexual learning begins with agency: the ability to make choices about your own body and participation. You are welcome here whether you are sexually active, curious, uncertain, experienced, inexperienced or uninterested in particular activities. A positive approach to sexuality includes wellbeing, respect and freedom from coercion; it does not require anyone to have more sex. The World Health Organization places these ideas within sexual health. [A04]

The Academy's ethical standard is that every person actively and freely agrees to the specific activity, understands relevant conditions, can make the decision, and remains free to stop. Consent concerns the present situation. A previous yes, a relationship, a gift, flirting or attraction cannot supply today's answer. Agreement to one activity also does not cover another activity, recording, or a change to an agreed barrier method. Australian Government consent guidance supports active, ongoing agreement and explains that its community definition is distinct from state and territory law. [A01]

Think of an invitation as a question whose answer belongs to the other person. If you would become angry, keep asking, withdraw essential support or make the person prove their affection after a no, the invitation is carrying pressure. A respectful invitation makes a decline usable: the conversation and the person's dignity survive it.

Specific language helps. “Would you like a kiss?” gives clearer information than “Are you okay with everything?” A response can be communicated through words, an agreed communication aid or another clear method that both people understand. Do not turn silence or ambiguity into permission. Ask, allow time, and accept uncertainty as a reason to pause.

Consent also belongs to you. You may stop an activity you suggested, decline something you usually enjoy, or decide that you want closeness without sexual contact. You do not need an impressive explanation. The same freedom applies to everyone involved, including people whose wishes differ from yours.

Use two questions to test your practice: “What exactly have we agreed to?” and “Is it genuinely easy for each person to change their mind?” If either answer is unclear, create clarity before proceeding. This is a practical ethical standard, not a substitute for checking the applicable law.

lessons.title: Capacity, access and freedom from pressure
objectives: Identify situations in which a freely made decision is not established.
Separate a person's communication access needs from assumptions about their capacity.
Choose a pause when intoxication, dependency or power makes consent uncertain.
lessons.content:
A yes has meaning only when the person can choose it. Consider three questions: can they understand the proposed activity and its relevant conditions; can they communicate their decision in a way you both understand; and can they decline without fear or penalty? These questions guide the Academy's practice. They are not a legal test or a way to diagnose another person's capacity.

Do not begin or continue sexual activity with someone who is asleep, unconscious, or too affected by alcohol or other drugs to understand, decide or communicate. If you cannot establish that they can freely choose, stop and wait for a situation where that is clear. Never use intoxication as a method of obtaining agreement. 1800RESPECT identifies pressure, impaired capacity and lack of alertness as barriers to consent. [A02]

A disability, a diagnosis, limited speech or an unfamiliar communication style does not by itself tell you what someone understands or wants. People with cognitive disability have sexual lives and relationship interests, and disability services should support choice, dignity and accessible communication. [A05, A06] Offer time, plain language or a communication aid selected by the person. A support person's convenience or interpretation must not replace the adult's own decision.

Pressure can be quiet. An adult may worry about losing a home, employment, care, money or acceptance. Ask yourself whether you control something the person depends on. “They said yes” does not answer whether refusing felt safe. Professional care and authority relationships require particular boundaries and may also be subject to specific legal or professional restrictions; this lesson does not establish an exception to them.

Make alternatives real. If someone depends on you for a ride, provide the agreed ride without attaching intimacy to it. If you are disappointed, manage that feeling without making it their problem to solve. If the situation cannot support a free decision, do not try to engineer a better-sounding yes.

When another adult is confused or significantly impaired, prioritise immediate safety and nonsexual care. If they cannot be woken, are unconscious, have abnormal breathing or are having a seizure, call 000 and ask for an ambulance. Follow the operator's instructions rather than waiting for them to recover unaided. [H01, H02] If they can communicate, ask what support they want. Meaningful choice is the condition for participation, and pausing protects it.

lessons.title: Check in, stop and respond with care
objectives: Use clear check-ins before and during an interaction.
Respond promptly when someone withdraws, freezes or becomes uncertain.
Describe an accountable response after a boundary has been crossed.
lessons.content:
Consent is a continuing conversation, not a completed form. People can change their minds, and physical arousal does not prove agreement. Silence, hesitation or freezing should not be interpreted as permission to continue. These points are explicit in Australian Government consent education. [A01] The Academy's practical response to uncertainty is to stop the activity and check what the person wants next.

A useful check-in offers meaningful choices. “Would you like to keep going, change something, or stop?” is clearer than a hurried “You're fine, right?” Leave enough time for an answer. For someone who uses a communication aid, make sure it remains available. Agreeing on a word or signal can help communication, but nobody must use a special phrase to earn the right to stop.

If a person says stop, moves away, goes still or seems disconnected, stop first. Reduce pressure and ask a simple question such as “Would you like space?” Do not insist on touch, explanations or eye contact. Reassurance should not become another demand: the person does not have to comfort you or say that everything is all right.

Later, a conversation may be useful if the other person wants one. Name your action accurately: “I continued after you pulled away. I should have stopped.” Listen without correcting their feelings. An apology becomes more meaningful when behaviour changes, including respecting requests for distance. A good intention does not cancel an impact. Equally, this course cannot determine the legal meaning of a specific event.

If you are the person who became uncomfortable, you may leave, ask for support, stay quiet or take time before deciding what you want to do. You do not need to organise the perfect response. Freezing or finding it difficult to speak does not transfer responsibility to you. For confidential support about sexual violence or abuse in Australia, contact 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732 or use its website. [A02]

Practise this pattern in everyday life: ask before borrowing, notice hesitation, return the item when asked, and respond without punishment. The point is not to perform flawless phrases. It is to build a habit in which another person's change of mind reliably changes what you do.

modules.title: Communication and boundaries
modules.summary: Practise clear requests, useful listening, everyday boundaries and separate consent for digital participation.

lessons.title: Ask clearly and listen to the answer
objectives: Make a specific invitation without building in the expected answer.
Use a brief listening and clarification sequence.
Adapt communication to access needs without taking over another person's decision.
lessons.content:
Communication becomes more useful when it reduces the amount another person must guess. “I would like some time together this weekend. Would Saturday suit you?” identifies a wish and offers a choice. The same principle applies to conversations about intimacy: name the topic, ask whether now is a good time, and make room for an answer you did not predict. WA Health's consent education emphasises assertive communication and respectful responses to a no. [A03]

Try a three-part conversation. First, describe your own preference: “I would like us to talk about what we both enjoy.” Next, ask an open question: “What would make that conversation comfortable for you?” Finally, confirm the answer in plain language: “So you would prefer to talk tomorrow, without trying anything tonight.” Confirmation checks understanding; it is not a promise that either person must follow through later.

Listening does not mean silently preparing your rebuttal. Let the person finish, reflect the point they made and ask whether you have understood. If a phrase is vague, clarify it without turning the conversation into an interrogation. “When you say private, do you mean no photos, no sharing with friends, or something else?” is more useful than assuming you already share the same definition.

People communicate in different ways. Written messages, speech, pictures or communication devices may make a conversation more accessible. NDIS practice standards recognise communication methods, privacy and informed choice. [A06] Ask what works for the person, use one question at a time where helpful, and allow processing time. Slow communication is not less adult communication.

Timing matters. A conversation started during an argument, while rushing out the door or when someone is impaired may not allow thoughtful choices. Suggest another time without using delay as punishment. A planned conversation can cover preferences and safety, while each later interaction still needs consent.

Your goal is shared understanding, not a perfect script or a favourable answer. A successful discussion may reveal that two people want different things. Knowing that difference early creates useful options: choose an activity everyone wants, agree to revisit the subject without pressure, or accept that the proposed interaction will not happen.

lessons.title: Boundaries, requests and incompatibility
objectives: Distinguish a personal boundary, a request and controlling behaviour.
Respond to a boundary without bargaining or punishment.
Recognise that an incompatibility can exist without either adult being wrong.
lessons.content:
A boundary describes the conditions under which you will participate and the choices you will make for yourself. A request asks another person to consider an action. Control attempts to remove the other person's freedom. “I will not lend my phone” is a boundary. “Would you put your phone away during dinner?” is a request. “You must give me your passwords so I can inspect your conversations” raises a different issue: one person claiming authority over the other's privacy.

Healthy relationships allow safety, respect and independence. WA Government guidance describes the ability to discuss feelings without fear and make personal decisions without another person controlling them. [A32] These principles apply to a new date, a long partnership, a friendship and a relationship that does not fit a conventional label.

Make boundaries understandable. State what you are and are not agreeing to, using the detail needed for that situation. “I do not want photos taken” is clearer than “Be respectful.” You may offer an alternative if you want one, but an alternative is optional. A no does not become incomplete because it lacks a substitute.

When you hear a limit, acknowledge it before discussing anything else. “Understood; I will not do that” is a useful response. Feeling disappointed is different from making disappointment a consequence the other person must manage. Sulking, repeated requests, insults, threatening withdrawal of care or using a person's vulnerability to change their answer undermine free choice.

Sometimes two adults want incompatible arrangements. One may want monogamy while the other does not; one may want frequent contact while the other wants more independence. Neither needs to agree to an arrangement they do not want. The available choices may include a different agreement, more time, or ending the relationship respectfully. Compromise is useful only where each person freely wants the resulting arrangement.

A boundary can also change. Revisiting it means checking the current preference, not presenting a case until it collapses. Decide together whether and when a later conversation is welcome. Until then, act on the existing limit. Someone else's boundary is information about their participation, not an invitation to measure your skill at persuasion.

lessons.title: Digital consent and personal privacy
objectives: Separate consent to receive, create, keep and share intimate media.
Recognise that a private message is not permission for a new audience.
Identify a practical support route for image-based abuse.
lessons.content:
Digital intimacy includes messages, live calls, photographs, recordings and AI-altered media. Treat each step as a separate decision. Agreeing to flirt does not mean agreeing to receive a sexual image. Agreeing to a private call does not mean agreeing to recording. A person who appears in an image has a say in how it is used; being someone's partner does not create ownership of their likeness.

eSafety defines image-based abuse as sharing, or threatening to share, an intimate image or video without the person's consent. Sending an image to one person does not authorise that person to show it to others. This applies even if the original image was willingly created or sent. [A08] The Academy also requires specific permission before creating a sexualised edit or AI representation of an identifiable adult; a public photograph is not that permission.

Before any digital participation, ask what is being proposed, who can see it, whether anything will be saved, and what each person wants if circumstances change. Avoid promising that an app makes copying impossible. A disappearing message should not be treated as proof that no copy can exist. Decide what you are comfortable creating in light of uncertainty, and respect a decision to create nothing.

Privacy is broader than images. A partner's diagnosis, orientation, relationship structure or attendance on a sexuality course is not casual gossip material. You can seek support about your own experience while limiting identifying details about others. When a professional needs information, ask what will be recorded and how confidentiality works.

If an intimate image is shared or threatened without permission, responsibility rests with the person misusing it. You can seek help from eSafety's reporting service. If safe, follow its guidance on preserving relevant links and evidence; you do not have to circulate the image to prove what happened. eSafety can help with removal requests and threats, but no service should be treated as a guarantee that every copy will disappear. [A09]

For Academy exercises, use fictional examples and keep private reflections out of public discussions. Learning about sexual communication should never require uploading a nude, naming partners, revealing a diagnosis or demonstrating sexual activity.

lessons.title: Anatomy without assumptions
objectives: Distinguish the vulva from the vagina and identify common reproductive structures.
Identify common penile and testicular structures using accurate terms.
Avoid inferring identity, preferences or consent from anatomy.
lessons.content:
Anatomical language helps people describe a symptom, ask a question or communicate a boundary. These words are tools, not tests of gender or experience. You may use different words for your own body. In a healthcare conversation, pairing your preferred term with a familiar anatomical term can help a clinician understand you accurately.

The vulva is the external genital region, including the labia, clitoris and the openings of the urethra and vagina. The vagina is an internal canal leading to the cervix. The cervix forms the lower part of the uterus; ovaries produce hormones and contain eggs. The urethral opening and the vaginal opening are separate. [A10, A12]

The penis includes the shaft and glans. The scrotum is the skin sac containing the testes, which produce sperm and hormones. The prostate and other glands contribute fluid to semen. The urethra carries urine from the bladder and, in a penis, also carries semen at a different time. [A11] Reproductive functions, urinary functions and pleasurable sensations are related in some structures but are not interchangeable concepts.

These descriptions outline common arrangements. They do not mean that every person has every listed organ. Bodies can differ because of innate variations, surgery, injury or other circumstances. Intersex refers to variations in sex characteristics; it does not identify a person's gender or sexual orientation. NSW Health recommends language that respects both bodily diversity and the person's own preferences. [A13]

Do not turn an anatomy lesson into a prediction about another adult. A person's body does not tell you which activities they enjoy, whether they are fertile, how they describe themselves, or what touch they welcome. An organ's possible function is not an obligation to use it in a particular way. Questions about someone else's anatomy should have a relevant purpose and their permission.

When you need to communicate, use a precise location and an ordinary description: “I have discomfort at the vaginal entrance” or “I noticed swelling in the scrotum.” A clinician can then ask useful follow-up questions. You do not need to memorise a diagram before seeking care.

For learning, labelled medical diagrams are enough. This course never needs a photograph of your body. Aim to leave with clearer vocabulary and fewer assumptions, rather than a checklist against which anyone's body must be judged.

lessons.title: Variation, sensation and body image
objectives: Recognise ordinary variation without using one appearance as an ideal.
Separate respect for a body from pressure to feel positively about it.
Distinguish appearance comparisons from a change that warrants health advice.
lessons.content:
A body is not a standardised product. Genitals vary in size, shape and colour, and two sides need not be identical. NSW Health's Play Safe resource specifically explains that labia can be asymmetrical and can extend beyond the outer labia. [A12] A simplified diagram illustrates a structure; it does not show every healthy way that structure can look.

Innate variations in sex characteristics are another part of bodily diversity. These may involve anatomy, chromosomes or hormones and may be recognised at different stages of life. They do not prescribe a person's identity or relationships. [A14] Nobody is obliged to disclose a variation, medical history or surgery simply because another person is curious.

Appearance comparisons often ask an unhelpful question: “Do I match the image?” Replace it with questions about comfort, function and change. “Is this new for me?” and “Is it causing discomfort?” are more useful reasons to seek advice. A familiar difference and a new painful swelling should not be treated as the same thing. Respecting variation does not mean ignoring symptoms or trying to diagnose yourself from photographs.

You do not have to love every part of your body to treat it with care. A neutral statement such as “This is my body, and it deserves comfort and healthcare” can be more accessible than forced confidence. You may have complicated feelings about scars, body hair, size, ageing, disability or gendered language. This lesson does not ask you to resolve those feelings or display your body to anyone.

The same approach matters with partners. Avoid ranking body types or assuming that a feature predicts sensation or sexual skill. Ask what feels comfortable and which words the person prefers. Feedback about an interaction is more useful than a claim about how a body should work. A respectful response to a difference is curiosity with permission, not surprise treated as a public event.

If a body concern is persistent, distressing or linked to symptoms, a qualified clinician can help distinguish ordinary variation from a health issue. You can request an explanation in plain language and discuss options before making a decision. The aim of body literacy is informed care and autonomy, not conformity to an aesthetic template.

lessons.title: Body care and getting useful health support
objectives: Describe gentle, proportionate genital hygiene without treating natural variation as dirt.
Identify symptoms that need clinical attention and an example requiring emergency assessment.
Prepare a clear, private question for a sexual-health consultation.
lessons.content:
Genital care does not require making the body scentless or matching an advertisement. The vagina has its own cleaning processes; routine internal washing or douching is unnecessary and can cause problems. Keep external care gentle and avoid products that irritate your skin. Public health guidance advises washing the external genital area and avoiding douches inside the vagina. [A17] If a clinician has prescribed specific care for a condition or procedure, follow that individual advice.

Pain, irritation or a new change is information. Persistent itching, sores, swelling, unusual discharge, pain when urinating or unexpected bleeding deserve a discussion with a health professional. Symptoms can have different causes, so do not assume that every irritation is an STI or that a familiar remedy is appropriate. Healthdirect recommends assessment for new or persistent groin irritation and infection. [A12, A15]

Some symptoms need urgent action. Sudden or severe testicular pain requires emergency medical assessment because time-sensitive conditions can cause it. [A16] This is a reason to seek emergency care, not to wait for a course discussion or attempt a diagnosis online. If you are unsure about other symptoms, use a local health advice service or contact a clinician.

Recurring pain associated with sex also deserves care. Do not make enduring pain a condition of being a good partner or proving that an activity is working. A clinician can investigate different physical and other contributing factors and discuss appropriate options. [A18] Stopping an activity is allowed while you decide what support you want.

Prepare a consultation using four pieces of information: where the concern is, when it began, what has changed, and what you want help with. You can write these down, use your preferred body language, or ask for an interpreter or communication support. Ask what an examination would involve and why it is being proposed. You can also ask whether a support person, chaperone or different clinician is available.

Useful healthcare questions include “What are the possible explanations?”, “Which tests would help?”, and “What should make me seek urgent help?” There is no need to give a polished performance. Accurate information and a respectful conversation help you make decisions without turning a symptom into a judgement about your character.

modules.title: Desire, arousal, pleasure and solo wellbeing
modules.summary: Understand sexual interest and bodily response without performance targets, shame or required sexual participation.

lessons.title: Desire is not the same as arousal
objectives: Distinguish sexual interest, bodily response and consent.
Recognise that desire can vary between people and across life circumstances.
Identify when a change in desire is a reason to seek support rather than self-blame.
lessons.content:
Desire describes interest in sexual activity. Arousal describes aspects of sexual response, including bodily changes. Consent is the person's freely communicated decision about participation. These concepts can relate to one another, but they cannot substitute for one another. A bodily response does not tell you that a person wants the activity, and Australian consent guidance explicitly rejects physical arousal as evidence of consent. [A01]

Libido varies between people and can change with relationships, health and life circumstances. Healthdirect describes possible influences including stress, medicines, hormonal changes and health concerns. [A19, A20] A comparison with another person cannot tell you what level is right for you. Nor does one encounter provide a reliable judgement about attraction, affection or the future of a relationship.

Notice the difference between “I would like more interest in sex for myself” and “Someone says I owe them more interest.” The first may lead to useful reflection or care. The second raises a question about pressure. A partner may express their own needs, but desire cannot be demanded as evidence of love. If people's wishes differ, each still controls their own participation.

Attraction, identity and behaviour are also distinct. Some people use asexual-spectrum language to describe little or no sexual attraction; others do not want a label. Sexuality includes feelings and attractions as well as behaviour. [A33] Do not diagnose an identity from a period of low desire or assume that an identity removes a person's ability to choose affection, relationships or sexual activities.

A practical reflection asks what creates comfort and what takes attention away: privacy, time, fatigue, stress, relationship tension or a health change. This is information gathering, not a recipe that guarantees arousal. You may choose closeness for its own sake without committing to a sexual outcome. If interest does not develop, the choice to stop remains complete.

If a change is persistent or distressing to you, speak with a qualified clinician. A review may consider physical health, medicines, relationships and other circumstances. Do not stop prescribed medication or begin hormone products because a course or advertisement promises a higher libido. The useful goal is wellbeing and informed choice, not reaching a universal target.

lessons.title: Pleasure without a performance target
objectives: Identify sexual scripts that turn an interaction into a performance test.
Use comfort, choice and communication as measures of an interaction's quality.
Respect differences in preferences without promising a specific bodily outcome.
lessons.content:
A sexual script is an expectation about how an interaction is supposed to unfold: who initiates, what counts as sex, what happens next, or which outcome proves success. Scripts can be useful when shared, but they become limiting when people mistake them for obligations. You can question a script without replacing it with a new rule that everyone must follow.

The World Health Organization's positive account of sexual health includes the possibility of pleasurable experiences alongside safety, respect and freedom from coercion. [A04] Possibility is not a performance requirement. A person can value affection, curiosity, erotic interest, emotional connection or solitude differently. No one must enjoy a particular activity to qualify as open-minded.

Pleasure is subjective. An activity enjoyed by one adult may be neutral or unwelcome to another. Orgasm is one possible sexual experience; it should not be treated as the only acceptable ending or a certificate of a partner's competence. Jean Hailes describes sexual wellbeing as involving pleasure, communication and factors that can affect arousal and orgasm. [A21] Ask for feedback without turning the answer into a review of your worth.

Try replacing “Did we do it right?” with more useful questions: “Did everyone want to be there?”, “Could we change direction?”, “Was discomfort taken seriously?”, and “What would each person choose next time?” These questions do not guarantee a particular sensation. They make room for honest information and shared responsibility.

Curiosity is also different from commitment. An adult may think about a fantasy, read about an activity, or ask a question without wanting to enact it. Learning is not consent. In the same way, declining one activity does not mean rejecting all closeness or rejecting the other person as a whole.

Comfort deserves attention. If an activity becomes painful or unwanted, stop rather than chasing a planned outcome. Recurring sexual pain can be assessed by a clinician. [A18] A change of plan, a laugh, a pause or a decision to end an interaction can all be signs of people using their agency well.

Bring this approach to your learning: be curious, keep your boundaries, and allow uncertainty. Progress means having better information and more usable choices, not collecting experiences or proving that you can tolerate everything.

lessons.title: Solo wellbeing, privacy and self-directed choice
objectives: Describe masturbation as an optional behaviour without a frequency target.
Distinguish private self-directed learning from involving another person.
Recognise functional concerns that may warrant nonjudgemental professional support.
lessons.content:
Solo sexual wellbeing means making informed choices about your own experience without needing a partner or an audience. Masturbation is self-stimulation for sexual pleasure. Some adults choose it; some do not. Victoria's Better Health Channel describes it as a personal choice and notes that frequency differs between people. There is no course requirement to masturbate, view pornography or purchase a product. [A22]

The Academy treats curiosity and privacy as compatible. You can learn anatomical terms, reflect on what comfort means, or notice which messages create pressure without performing any sexual act. You can also decide that this topic is not relevant to you. Opting out does not make someone less informed, liberated or worthy of inclusion.

Privacy also protects other people. An activity stops being solely private if someone else is made to witness it, receive media of it or participate in a live interaction. Their consent becomes necessary. A shared home, online call or public setting should not be treated as an automatic audience. Consider ordinary arrangements for personal space without turning privacy into a demand that others surrender theirs.

If you choose to use a product, read the manufacturer's instructions and seek appropriate health advice if something causes irritation or pain. Do not treat a marketing claim as proof that a product is necessary for wellbeing. This lesson teaches decision-making, not a technique or a purchasing list.

Frequency alone is a poor way to judge a person's wellbeing. More useful concerns include unwanted interference with work, sleep, responsibilities or relationships, or distress and difficulty controlling behaviour. Better Health Channel advises seeking professional support when masturbation interferes with everyday life or causes concern. [A22] Support should help clarify what is happening rather than impose shame or an arbitrary quota.

For a private reflection, ask: “Is this my choice?”, “Does it fit with the rest of my life?”, and “Am I treating myself and other people with care?” You may answer with fictional examples. Learning about sexuality does not require providing a history to a teacher.

A self-directed approach leaves room for different values. Someone can enjoy solo activity, prefer partnered connection, choose both, or choose neither. The shared standard is informed choice, privacy and respect.

modules.title: Safer sex, sexual health and contraception
modules.summary: Combine prevention options, appropriate testing, pregnancy prevention and timely help after an exposure or contraceptive problem.

lessons.title: Build a practical prevention plan
objectives: Explain why prevention combines several measures rather than one guarantee.
Distinguish STI risk reduction from pregnancy prevention.
Identify questions about barriers, vaccination and HIV prevention to discuss with a clinician.
lessons.content:
Safer sex is a shared planning process. Start with the activities being considered, the body parts involved, relevant health information and each person's boundaries. An orientation or relationship label is not a substitute for that conversation. Nobody's appearance establishes their STI status, and a prevention discussion should describe practical information without labelling people as clean or dirty.

Different infections spread through different kinds of contact. Barriers can reduce exposure during vaginal, anal or oral sexual activity, but they do not remove every risk, including contact with uncovered skin. Australia's STI prevention guidance recommends combining barriers, testing, communication and appropriate vaccination. It also explains that hormonal contraception does not prevent STIs. [A23]

External condoms, internal condoms and dental dams have different intended uses. Read the package instructions, check the expiry date and use a new barrier each time as directed. Do not use an external and internal condom together. Use a compatible lubricant and follow the product's instructions; water- or silicone-based condom-safe lubricant can help reduce tearing. [A23, A24] If a material irritates you, ask a pharmacist or clinician about suitable alternatives rather than assuming all barriers are unsuitable.

Agree on barrier use before the activity, and keep that agreement in place. A change is a new decision for everyone affected. If a barrier fails, pause and discuss what happened without blame. Depending on the situation, time-sensitive pregnancy prevention, HIV prevention or other health advice may be relevant; the next lessons explain those routes.

Ask a clinician whether your hepatitis B and HPV vaccinations are up to date. Vaccines protect against specific infections, not all STIs. PrEP is medicine used before possible HIV exposure for people for whom it is appropriate; it is different from PEP, which is considered after an exposure. [A23, A34] Neither name should be treated as a general guarantee about sexual health or as permission to change a partner's boundary.

A useful plan names what you will use, who will obtain it, how you will communicate a change, and where you can get advice. It also includes the option to choose another activity or stop. Planning does not make intimacy less spontaneous; it reduces the amount of important information that must be guessed.

U=U means undetectable equals untransmittable: a person living with HIV who takes treatment as prescribed and maintains an undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV through sex. This does not prevent other STIs or remove anyone’s consent and barrier preferences. [R17]

lessons.title: Testing, results and conversations without stigma
objectives: Explain why symptoms and appearance cannot reliably establish STI status.
Describe how timing, test type and sampled body sites affect interpretation.
Use a practical, nonjudgemental conversation about testing and follow-up.
lessons.content:
Many STIs do not produce noticeable symptoms. Testing can identify infections that a person would otherwise miss. The Australian Government recommends discussing test frequency and relevant risk factors with a healthcare professional rather than relying on appearance or relationship status. A consultation may involve urine, blood or swab samples depending on what needs checking. [A25]

lessons.title: Contraception and time-sensitive care
objectives: Compare broad contraception choices using personal needs rather than a universal best method.
Identify prompt help after possible pregnancy or HIV exposure.
Explain why emergency contraception and HIV PEP address different risks.
lessons.content:
Pregnancy prevention is relevant when the bodies and activity involved could allow sperm to reach an egg. Discuss that possibility directly rather than guessing from gender, orientation or relationship labels. Contraception is the choice of the person whose body uses the method; a partner can share practical responsibility without taking control of that decision.

Options include condoms, pills, implants, injections, intrauterine devices and other methods. They differ in how they are used, how long they last, side effects, suitability and how easy it is to stop or change them. Healthdirect's Contraception Options Finder helps people compare options using their needs and preferences. [A29, A30] A clinician or pharmacist can explain medical suitability and interactions. No course can select the best method for every learner.

Long-acting reversible methods include implants and IUDs. A trained clinician inserts and removes them. Some people value not having a daily task; others prefer a method they manage differently. [A28] A choice should be informed and voluntary. Sabotaging contraception or pressuring someone about pregnancy is incompatible with the Academy's consent standard.

If contraception fails or sex creates a pregnancy concern, seek advice promptly. In Australia, emergency contraceptive pills are available from pharmacies without a prescription. Levonorgestrel is generally used within 72 hours; ulipristal acetate can be used within 120 hours. A copper IUD can also be an emergency option within five days, with clinical assessment and insertion. Timing, medicines and other individual factors affect the choice, so contact a pharmacist or clinician as soon as possible. Emergency contraceptive pills delay or prevent ovulation; they do not treat an established pregnancy. [A27, A28]

Possible HIV exposure is a separate time-sensitive issue. PEP is prescribed medicine taken after an exposure and should be started as soon as possible, within 72 hours. Seek urgent advice from a sexual-health service or emergency department; do not wait for symptoms or a test result. [A34] Emergency contraception does not prevent HIV, and PEP does not prevent pregnancy.

After urgent advice, ask when to start or restart your regular contraceptive method, how long to use condoms or avoid sex that could cause pregnancy, and when a pregnancy test is needed. Starting progestogen-containing contraception too soon after ulipristal acetate can reduce its effectiveness; a five-day delay is generally advised. Obtain instructions for your specific method, including protection until it becomes effective. Emergency contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy from later sex. [H03] If more time has passed, still seek advice about options and follow-up. You can seek care even if you feel embarrassed, are uncertain about what happened, or have missed a usual prevention step.

modules.title: Relationships and agreements
modules.summary: Create clear, voluntary agreements, work with disagreement and recognise when care, distance or specialist support is needed.

lessons.title: Choose agreements, not assumptions
objectives: Describe a relationship agreement without treating a label as a full specification.
Identify areas that need explicit discussion and consent from affected adults.
Recognise that an agreement cannot provide permanent sexual permission.
lessons.content:
Adults organise relationships in different ways. Some choose monogamy; some agree to non-monogamy; some prefer casual connections, friendship, partnership without sex or being single. The Academy does not rank these arrangements. Its standard is that affected adults have enough relevant information to make voluntary choices and are treated with care. Respect and safety are central to healthy relationships. [A07]

A label is a conversation starter. “Exclusive”, “open”, “casual” and “partner” can mean different things to different people. Ask what the term means in practice: which commitments are being made, what information should be shared, how time is organised, and what would count as a change requiring another discussion. Do not assume an agreement from relationship duration or the intensity of someone's feelings.

Separate three things. A personal boundary concerns your participation. A shared agreement describes commitments each person freely accepts. A request invites an action that the other person may decline. Clear distinctions help prevent an agreement from becoming a rule imposed on someone who was never asked. In a relationship involving several adults, one person's permission cannot stand in for another person's consent.

Privacy requires attention too. Relevant health or agreement changes may need to be communicated without revealing unnecessary intimate details about a third person. Ask what information helps someone make their own decision and whether you have permission to share it. Avoid using disclosure as surveillance or requiring photographs and messages as routine proof of loyalty.

Make agreements concrete enough to use. For example: “If a change affects our agreed health precautions, we will discuss it before further sexual contact.” Decide how a difficult conversation can be initiated and what happens while the issue is unresolved. A pause can be an agreed way to protect choices while people obtain information.

Review agreements when circumstances change. An adult can decide that an arrangement no longer works for them, and another adult can decide that the proposed change does not work for them. Renegotiation does not guarantee agreement. Even a written relationship agreement never supplies permanent consent to sexual activity. The purpose is mutual understanding that can be acted on honestly, including the possibility that people choose different paths.

lessons.title: Jealousy, disagreement and renegotiation
objectives: Express a difficult feeling without treating it as authority over another adult.
Use a structured conversation about a specific disagreement.
Distinguish ordinary disagreement from patterns of fear and coercive control.
lessons.content:
Difficult feelings do not make someone bad at relationships. Jealousy, insecurity, disappointment and uncertainty can prompt useful questions about needs and expectations. A feeling is real, but it does not automatically identify the cause or decide what another person must do. You can acknowledge the feeling while taking responsibility for the action you choose next.

Start with a specific observation rather than a character judgement: “Our plans changed twice this week” is easier to discuss than “You never care.” Name the effect on you and make a concrete request: “I felt unsettled; could we agree on how to communicate changes?” Then listen. The other person's account may add information without erasing your experience.

For a difficult conversation, agree on a time, define one issue and give each person space to describe their view. Summarise the points of agreement and the remaining difference. Ask whether there is an option both freely want. If emotions make useful listening difficult, propose a pause and, where safe, a realistic time to revisit the subject. A pause should not be used to punish someone with uncertainty.

Renegotiating is not retroactive permission. If someone wants to change an agreement, raise it before acting on the change. If an agreement has already been broken, acknowledge that fact and discuss the relevant consequences, including health information or a need for distance. Do not demand immediate forgiveness or use the discussion to obtain unwanted sexual reassurance.

There is a difference between disagreement and a pattern that makes someone afraid. Repeated monitoring, isolation, threats, control of money or restriction of healthcare can be part of coercive control. 1800RESPECT describes this as a pattern used to dominate and control another person. [A31] Better communication phrases do not make such a pattern safe, and the targeted person is not responsible for fixing it through a better conversation.

If fear or control is present, seek individual support from a specialist service rather than treating a joint discussion as the only next step. You can contact 1800RESPECT for help considering options. [A31] Relationship skills should increase each person's freedom to choose; they should never become a reason to remain in a situation that feels unsafe.

lessons.title: Care, repair and respectful endings
objectives: Offer care without assuming which response another adult wants.
Describe accountability that does not demand forgiveness or renewed intimacy.
Plan an ending that respects boundaries, privacy and safety.
lessons.content:
Care continues after an interaction and during changes to a relationship. It begins with asking rather than assuming. One person may want a conversation, another may want ordinary company, and another may prefer privacy. “Would you like company, practical help or space?” offers choices. The answer can change, and offering care does not create permission for touch or access.

A follow-up conversation can ask what worked, what did not and what needs to change. Keep the focus on information and behaviour. “I noticed that we rushed the discussion about plans” is more useful than inviting a rating of someone's performance. No one has to provide a full explanation of a difficult feeling before being allowed a boundary.

Repair requires accountability. If you broke an agreement, name the action, communicate any information relevant to the other person's health or choices, and follow through on practical changes. Listen to the impact without making the conversation about obtaining reassurance. An apology can be offered; forgiveness, continued contact and renewed intimacy cannot be collected as payment for it.

Sometimes a relationship ends. A respectful ending makes practical matters clear: the return of belongings, access to shared accounts, future contact, private information and any outstanding health communication. Discuss what is appropriate and feasible without treating a final meeting, a hug or sexual contact as something owed. A person may decline further conversation even if the other person wants closure.

Privacy obligations do not disappear at a breakup. Do not share intimate images, private diagnoses or identifying stories to recruit an audience against the other person. eSafety explains that sharing or threatening to share intimate images without consent is image-based abuse, including after a relationship ends. [A08]

Where threats, stalking, violence or coercive control are involved, a direct in-person ending may not be the safest option. Specialist support can help someone consider a plan suited to their circumstances. 1800RESPECT advises supporting people's safety and choice without ordering them to leave in a particular way. [A31] In immediate danger in Australia, call 000.

The skill is to hold care and autonomy together. You can take responsibility, grieve a loss, ask for support and respect another adult's decision at the same time. A relationship's ending does not erase the importance of dignity.

modules.title: Inclusive intimacy
modules.summary: Make room for diverse identities, bodies and relationships without making assumptions or requiring anyone to disclose.

lessons.title: Identity without assumptions
objectives: Distinguish sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.
Replace stereotypes with respectful, relevant questions.
Recognise that labels never provide consent or predict preferences.
lessons.content:
An inclusive approach starts with the person in front of you. Sexual orientation describes aspects of attraction; gender identity describes someone's experience of gender; sex characteristics concern bodily features. These ideas may relate in a person's life, but one does not tell you the others. Intersex describes innate variations of sex characteristics and is not a synonym for being transgender or non-binary. People may use several identity words, different words in different settings, or none. [B01, B02]

Treat a label as information someone has chosen to offer, not a complete instruction manual. A bisexual person has not promised attraction to everyone. A gay or straight label does not specify activities or relationship agreements. An asexual person may have their own preferences about romance, touch, relationships and sex. An aromantic person may value closeness without seeking a romantic relationship. You do not need to question or test someone's identity to understand a boundary.

Ask questions that matter to the decision being made. “What name and pronouns would you like me to use?” is different from requesting a transition history. “What kind of connection are you looking for?” is more useful than deciding what a person should want based on appearance. “Would you like to talk about touch?” creates room to decline the conversation itself. Allow a person time to answer; an immediate answer is not a condition of respect.

Learning a new term may take practice. If you use the wrong word, make a brief correction and continue using the person's words. Avoid asking them to reassure you that you are a good person. If a term is unfamiliar, learn from reputable community resources at another time. One individual should not have to represent an entire community.

Inclusive intimacy also leaves room for incompatibility. Respecting someone's identity does not require dating, attraction, sex or agreement to every request. Equally, declining a connection does not justify ridicule, outing or dehumanising explanations. You can say, “That connection is not right for me,” and still treat someone with dignity. The practical standard is ordinary and demanding: ask, listen, respect the answer, and avoid turning your assumptions into someone else's obligation.

objectives: Explain why bodies cannot be inferred from identity or appearance.
Use optional, specific language conversations to support comfort.
Respect intersex people's privacy and bodily autonomy.
lessons.content:
Bodies vary. So do the words people use for them, the kinds of touch they welcome, and the information they wish to share. Avoid treating one body as the standard that everyone else must explain. A respectful conversation begins with choice: “Are there words you prefer for your body?” or “Is there anything you would like me to avoid?” A person can answer briefly, change an answer later, or keep a topic private. Guidance developed for partners of trans and gender diverse people emphasises respect for body language and individual consent. [B03]

Intersex people have innate variations of sex characteristics. These can involve features such as hormones, chromosomes or reproductive anatomy, and people may discover a variation at different stages of life. Intersex people have diverse genders, orientations and preferred terms. There is no single intersex body or experience. Respect a person's chosen language rather than assigning a label or asking invasive questions. [B02]

Think about relevance before asking. An intimate partner may need a conversation about agreed activities, comfort, prevention or pregnancy possibilities. They do not automatically need a diagnosis, surgical history, photographs or explanation of how someone's body developed. You can establish a boundary without explaining its origin: “Please do not touch that area” is enough. If important health questions cannot be resolved comfortably, pause the proposed activity and seek appropriate advice together only if each person wants to.

Separate everyday language from clinical clarity. A person can use affirming body words with partners while asking a clinician to explain which anatomy is relevant to a particular test or symptom. Good preparation might be a note saying, “These are my preferred words; please ask before an examination and explain each step.” An educational platform cannot determine what screening or treatment is appropriate from someone's gender alone.

Curiosity becomes intrusive when another person's body is treated as an exhibit. If someone discloses an intersex variation or a transition experience, thank them for trusting you and ask what, if anything, they want from you. Do not share the information with others. A supportive response creates space for ordinary intimacy, humour and connection while leaving control over the body and the story with its owner.

objectives: Recognise outing and stereotyping as barriers to safety.
Identify practical signs of affirming support.
Plan a respectful response to a disclosure or identity-related mistake.
lessons.content:
Belonging is practical. It appears in forms that let someone use their name, examples that include different relationships, and conversations where nobody must defend their existence. It also appears in what is kept private. Being open with one partner, friend or clinician does not mean being open with every family member, colleague or online audience. Ask before sharing identity information, relationship details, images or attendance at this course.

Try a context question: “What name and words should I use here, and is anything private in this setting?” This is especially useful when moving from a private conversation to a group or public event. Respect the answer without pressing for an explanation. A person may be protecting safety, employment, family relationships or simply their preference for privacy. You do not have to decide whether their reason is sufficient.

Healthcare can be another place where assumptions get in the way. Australian health policy recognises stigma and barriers affecting LGBTIQA+ people and prioritises safe, inclusive care. [B01] When selecting a service, look for clear privacy information, respectful intake questions and a way to explain communication or access needs. An inclusive logo is a starting point; the experience of being listened to matters more. You may ask whether the practitioner has relevant experience and how they handle complaints or referrals.

You can prepare a small appointment note with a preferred name, relevant symptoms, words you would like used and questions you want answered. You may request explanations before examinations and ask about choices, including a support person where possible. You do not need to educate a practitioner about every aspect of your identity before asking for help.

For Australians who want an anonymous conversation, QLife provides free LGBTIQ+ peer support and referral around sexuality, gender, bodies and relationships. Check the service's website for current availability. [B04] Peer support, clinical treatment and emergency care serve different purposes; choosing one does not commit you to the others.

modules.title: Access and changing bodies
modules.summary: Make intimacy accessible across disability, neurodivergence, chronic conditions and life changes, with autonomy and individual care at the centre.

lessons.title: Access is part of consent
objectives: Distinguish support for a decision from making it for someone.
Identify access adjustments that support communication and privacy.
Recognise when uncertainty requires pausing and seeking qualified guidance.
lessons.content:
Disabled adults have varied wishes about sex, touch, relationships and privacy, just as other adults do. Needing support with daily living does not by itself tell you whether someone wants intimacy or how they make decisions. Healthdirect's disability and sex guidance addresses sexual wellbeing, contraception and consent together. [B05] Start with the adult's expressed wishes, not another person's assumptions about what their life should include.

Access can change whether a conversation is genuinely usable. Someone may need plain language, captions, a communication device, a quiet space, an interpreter, more time, or one question at a time. Ask which support works for them. A speech difference, lack of eye contact or slower response is not permission to ignore a person. Equally, do not guess at agreement when communication is unclear. Pause and establish a method both people understand.

Supported decision-making means helping a person understand options and communicate their own choice. It does not mean obtaining a support worker's or family member's approval in place of that adult's agreement. Consent and legal capacity questions can be context-specific; this course cannot assess an individual's capacity or authorise someone else to decide for them. If understanding or voluntariness remains uncertain, do not proceed. Seek appropriate specialist advice while continuing to treat the person respectfully.

Privacy is an access need too. Ask before a helper enters, before private information is repeated, or before a device is handled. A communication aid should not become a route for someone else to answer on the adult's behalf. Professional support relationships also have safeguarding and conduct boundaries; do not treat dependence on a worker for essential care as evidence of free agreement to a personal sexual relationship.

For example, a fictional learner may understand a consent discussion best through picture choices and extra processing time. SECCA and SHFPACT provide consent resources in Easy English, Plain Language and pictures. [B06] The goal is not to produce a yes more efficiently. The goal is a clear, voluntary choice, including no, not now, or I am unsure. The same dignity applies whichever answer is given.

lessons.title: Sensory needs, energy and chronic conditions
objectives: Use direct communication without stereotyping neurodivergent people.
Plan adjustments around comfort, energy and access.
Distinguish self-knowledge from medical advice or a promise to participate.
lessons.content:
There is no universal neurodivergent way to communicate, and no single access plan works for every disabled or chronically ill person. Some adults prefer clear literal language, written choices, predictable timing or a quieter environment. Others prefer different approaches. The National Autistic Society offers relationships and sexuality information for autistic adults, while healthdirect discusses individual sexual wellbeing with disability. [B07, B05] Use these resources to widen your questions, not to diagnose a partner or decide what they need without asking.

A useful conversation separates three things: interest, available energy and present comfort. Someone may want closeness but have little energy. They may enjoy one form of connection and dislike a particular sound, smell or kind of touch. They may change their mind when symptoms change. None of this needs to become a test of affection. “I would like company, and I need a quiet evening without touch” is a complete and workable request.

Plan access in ordinary language. Ask about lighting, noise, seating, room temperature, breaks, mobility needs and how to communicate a pause. A written message can be easier than a rapid conversation. Leave time to process without treating silence as agreement. If speech becomes difficult or the agreed communication method stops working, pause; an earlier plan cannot supply a new answer.

For chronic conditions, recovery or medicines, the person remains the expert on their own preferences, while a qualified clinician can advise about health risks and treatment. Do not recommend stopping medicines or ignoring symptoms to maintain a sexual schedule. A relevant question for a clinician might be, “Could my condition or treatment affect comfort, energy or sexual wellbeing, and what options are appropriate for me?” No one needs to provide a partner with their full medical record to request a break.

Keep plans flexible and easy to cancel. Offer an alternative only once, without turning every no into negotiations. Shared time, a conversation, separate rest or ending the evening can all be valid outcomes. Access is successful when people can make usable choices and have those choices respected, including a decision to do nothing sexual.

lessons.title: Changing bodies across adulthood
objectives: Recognise that readiness and preferences may change through life.
Describe menopause and postpartum care without gender assumptions.
Prepare a clinical question about a change in comfort or function.
lessons.content:
An adult body does not have to stay the same to deserve affection, respect or care. Ageing, illness, surgery, pregnancy, birth and hormonal changes can prompt new questions about comfort, energy and identity. Avoid using a previous version of your body as a performance target. The useful question is what supports wellbeing now, including whether you want sexual connection at all.

Menopause and its surrounding changes are not experiences limited to people who identify as women. Government guidance explains that trans, non-binary and gender diverse people born with ovaries may experience menopause, with timing and symptoms influenced by individual biology and medical care, including gender affirming care. [B08] Do not infer someone's experience from their name, gender or age. Ask a qualified clinician about new symptoms and how existing treatment affects the options; do not change hormones based on course material.

After giving birth, physical recovery, emotional readiness, feeding demands and tiredness can all affect intimacy. Pregnancy, Birth and Baby recommends listening to your body and considering your clinician's advice; a fixed date is not a requirement to resume sex. Healing and readiness vary. [B09] The same respect applies to trans and non-binary people who give birth. You can use words such as postpartum or birth recovery without imposing a parental title or gender.

In later adulthood, keep discussions individual. Do not assume that someone is uninterested in sex, automatically interested, incapable of decision-making, or free of sexual health concerns because of age. A changed relationship, bereavement or move into supported accommodation may make privacy and practical access especially relevant. Concern about a person's understanding requires an appropriate individual assessment, not a blanket rule based on age.

You can prepare for care by noting what has changed, when it started, what is uncomfortable and what you hope to improve. Ask about options and relevant sexual health or pregnancy prevention needs rather than guessing that these no longer apply. Seeking advice does not commit you to treatment or to sexual activity. Partners can help by sharing practical responsibilities, listening without taking changes personally, and making plans that can be paused. A comfortable conversation, rest or a new boundary can be meaningful progress.

Fertility may return before the first period after birth, including while breastfeeding. If avoiding pregnancy, discuss suitable contraception with a clinician. [R18]

modules.title: Exploring interests and kink literacy
modules.summary: Understand curiosity, negotiation, power, risk and aftercare without pressure to participate or instruction in hazardous practices.

lessons.title: Curiosity is not an obligation
objectives: Distinguish a private fantasy, a conversation and an agreement.
Use neutral vocabulary for sexual interests and kink.
Respond to an invitation or refusal without shame or pressure.
lessons.content:
Curiosity can take several forms: noticing an idea, imagining it, wanting information, discussing it, or considering participation. These are different decisions. You can be interested in understanding something without wanting to experience it. You can enjoy an imagined scenario while deciding that it does not belong in your real life. Sharing a fantasy never gives another person permission to act it out.

Kink is a broad community term for interests or practices perceived as outside conventional sexual expectations. BDSM is an umbrella abbreviation associated with bondage and discipline, dominance and submission, and sadism and masochism. These labels do not specify what any individual wants or has agreed to. Community consent education, including the NCSF Consent Counts programme, emphasises explicit communication; its US legal material is not Australian legal advice. [B10]

For learning, separate three categories: private thoughts; topics someone agrees to discuss; and activities everyone freely agrees to consider. Moving between categories needs another choice. “Would you be comfortable hearing about an interest?” asks for a conversation only. A yes to that conversation does not authorise images, demonstrations, touch, recording or participation. Describe a topic neutrally enough that someone can decide whether they want to hear more.

You may decline with a short sentence: “That is not something I want,” or “I am happy to discuss it, but I do not want to try it.” You do not owe an explanation that another person finds persuasive. Receive a no without bargaining, sulking or questioning whether someone is sufficiently adventurous. The government's consent guidance makes clear that preferences about taking control do not remove the need for ongoing agreement. [B11]

An open-minded learning environment leaves equal room for curiosity, firm limits and no interest in kink. It does not measure maturity by the range of activities someone accepts. Keep this lesson theoretical: your task is to identify decisions and respectful language. No disclosure of fantasies or participation in any sexual activity is needed to understand the material or complete the course.

lessons.title: Negotiation, power and stopping
objectives: Identify the decisions a negotiation must leave open.
Recognise how real-world power can undermine free choice.
Explain why a stop signal never replaces active attention.
lessons.content:
Negotiation is a conversation that may end with no activity taking place. Its purpose is to establish whether people's wishes, limits and circumstances are compatible. Start before an encounter, in a setting where each person can think clearly and leave freely. Discuss what is being proposed, what is excluded, relevant risks, privacy, and how to pause or stop. Keep the scope narrow enough that both people understand the same proposal.

Community negotiation resources can offer useful discussion prompts, but a checklist is not a waiver or permanent permission. [B10] A person may change their mind after a careful conversation. New information, discomfort, a changed environment or uncertainty may require stopping. Do not treat an earlier yes as an instruction to keep going until a particular word is spoken.

A stop plan should be simple and usable. Agree how each person will indicate pause or stop and what happens next. A familiar word or accessible signal can support communication, but ordinary refusals, pulling away, silence that creates uncertainty, or an inability to respond still require attention. If you cannot establish that someone wants to continue, stop. Anyone initiating or continuing contact must check that the other person wants it; a person experiencing distress is not responsible for performing a perfect refusal. [B11]

Distinguish an agreed role from real-world power. Someone who controls housing, wages, essential care or access to a community may make refusal feel costly. Reputation, experience and an instructor's authority can also create pressure. Calling the relationship consensual does not resolve those pressures. Ask whether saying no would genuinely be safe and whether each person can leave without punishment. If the answer is unclear, step back and seek independent support.

During this course, negotiation is practised through fictional conversations only. There is no requirement to create a sexual agreement, select a role or demonstrate an activity. A good result can be, “We want different things, so we will not proceed.” That is useful information, and no one needs to be blamed for it.

lessons.title: Risk awareness, aftercare and accountability
objectives: Recognise that consent does not remove physical risk.
Describe aftercare as a freely chosen support conversation.
Identify when stopping and professional help take priority.
lessons.content:
Consent and physical safety answer different questions. A person may freely want something that still carries serious risk. Enthusiasm, a checklist, a trusted partner or a course certificate cannot remove that risk. This lesson teaches how to recognise limits in your knowledge and decide when not to proceed. It does not teach restraints, injury-producing activities, drug use or other hazardous techniques.

Avoid neck compression, strangulation and restricting breathing during sexual activity. WA Health warns that pressure on the neck can be dangerous and fatal, including when described as consensual sexual activity. Harm may not be obvious from external marks. If neck compression has occurred, seek urgent medical assessment; call 000 for an emergency such as breathing difficulty, collapse or loss of consciousness. [B12] A stop word is not protection against an injury or an inability to speak.

For any proposed interest, ask what you do not know, whether there are health concerns needing qualified advice, and whether everyone can communicate and stop freely. Uncertainty can be a sufficient reason to decline. Do not use someone else's apparent confidence as evidence of competence. A social-media clip is not a safety assessment, and previous experiences without obvious harm do not guarantee the next outcome.

Aftercare means checking what support, space or follow-up someone wants after an experience. It might be a calm conversation, privacy or practical help, and preferences can differ. Ask rather than prescribing comfort. Someone who wants to leave should be able to leave. Do not insist on touch, emotional disclosure or reassurance as a condition of care.

Aftercare cannot turn a consent violation into a consensual event. If a limit was crossed, stop, attend to immediate needs, acknowledge what happened and respect the person's choices about contact and support. Seek professional assistance for injury or distress; do not frame symptoms as proof that an experience was successful. The learning goal is reliable judgment: knowing when to pause, refuse, get help or accept accountability is more valuable than collecting experiences.

modules.title: Digital intimacy
modules.summary: Apply consent to messages, images and AI likenesses; recognise manipulation and evaluate sexual media without shame or unrealistic expectations.

lessons.title: Messages, images and AI likenesses
objectives: Distinguish consent to receive, create, store and share intimate material.
Identify privacy questions before relying on an app feature.
Apply bodily autonomy to AI-generated or altered likenesses.
lessons.content:
Digital intimacy involves a series of separate choices. Someone may welcome flirting but not sexual images. They may agree to receive an image but not to appear in one. They may allow a private photograph but decline storage, editing, uploading or wider sharing. Ask before changing the audience or the use. Consent to one message or image does not establish continuing permission.

eSafety explains that sharing an intimate image with one person does not authorise that person to show or send it to others. Sharing or threatening to share intimate material without permission is image-based abuse, and the material can be real or digitally altered. [B13] A relationship ending does not turn private material into public property. Respect a request to stop sharing and discuss deletion honestly, without pretending that every copy elsewhere can be recovered.

Before relying on a service, check its current settings and policies. Can a recipient capture the screen? Are files automatically backed up? Can notifications expose content on a shared device? What happens if an account is compromised? A disappearing-message feature should not be treated as a promise that no copy can exist. Privacy controls support your choices but cannot guarantee another person's behaviour. Declining to create or send material is always an available choice.

AI adds new questions about likeness. A publicly available photograph is not ethical permission to create a sexualised version of its subject. Consent to ordinary photography is not consent to a sexual deepfake, voice imitation or simulated endorsement. eSafety's guidance recognises that AI-generated sexual imagery can be a form of image-based abuse. [B14] Seek specific, informed permission for each intended use of an identifiable adult's likeness, including generation, editing, storage, audience and commercial use.

Keep your own learning private too. This course never requires intimate uploads or access to a partner's accounts. A useful digital boundary can be simple: 'Please ask before sending explicit messages; no recording or sharing.' If someone violates it, the responsibility lies with their actions, not with your earlier trust or willingness to connect.

lessons.title: Scams, coercion and getting help
objectives: Recognise pressure and threats in a digital interaction.
Select appropriate first steps after sexual extortion.
Support a targeted person without blame or spreading their material.
lessons.content:
An online interaction can feel friendly and still become coercive. Pay attention when someone insists on secrecy, rushes trust, demands sexual material as proof of affection, or threatens consequences for declining. These patterns matter more than whether a profile looks convincing. You can slow down, leave a conversation or decline a request without proving that the other person is a scammer.

Sexual extortion, often called sextortion, involves threats to share intimate material unless demands are met. eSafety advises people not to pay or send more intimate content, to stop contact, and to seek help. Follow its current guidance on preserving useful evidence, reporting and blocking. [B15] If the threat involves immediate physical danger, contact emergency services. When an abusive partner may monitor devices, seek safety advice using a safer device if possible rather than making changes that could increase danger. [B26]

Practical evidence can include account names, dates, message details and links. Do not redistribute intimate material to classmates or friends to ask what they think. Keep any record private and follow the reporting service's instructions. Reporting options differ by the situation; eSafety can assess reports of image-based abuse and provides information on other appropriate services.
