lessons.title: Pornography and sexual media literacy
objectives: Separate entertainment and advertising from reliable education.
Identify missing information in a sexual media claim.
Make personal media choices without projecting them onto partners.
lessons.content:
Sexual media can include pornography, social posts, advertising, film and AI-generated scenes. Adults may make different choices about viewing it. This lesson asks you to evaluate what media can and cannot tell you. eSafety describes pornography as adult entertainment rather than sex education. [B16] A performance is not an instruction to copy, and an image cannot tell you what an individual partner wants.

Look for what is outside the frame. A clip may omit negotiation, preparation, breaks, editing, prevention measures or conversations afterward. You cannot confirm a participant's consent, comfort or working conditions merely from an expression on screen. The same limit applies to a creator's confidence: presentation quality is not evidence of medical expertise. A paid endorsement should prompt questions about incentives and evidence.

When you encounter a claim, ask four questions: Who made it? What evidence supports it? What has been left out? Does it apply to my question? For example, a promise that one product guarantees desire for everyone is too broad to guide individual care. A useful health resource explains limits and points to qualified help when needed. An educational discussion should also leave room for people who do not want the activity being described.

Notice when entertainment becomes a personal benchmark. Bodies, sounds, duration and visible responses may be selected or performed for an audience. There is no course target for looking a certain way or producing a particular response. You can replace comparison with a practical question: “What would make this interaction feel comfortable and chosen for the people involved?” The answer might be a conversation, a boundary or no sexual activity.

Discuss media preferences as a relationship conversation, not as an assumption. People can agree about shared viewing, privacy or what they want excluded from a conversation. Nobody must watch sexual material to prove openness, and a partner's fantasy preferences do not authorise real-life behaviour. Use this lesson's fictional examples only; no pornography viewing, intimate upload or disclosure of viewing habits is required to pass.

modules.title: When sex is difficult
modules.summary: Respond to pain, pressure, different desires and distress with autonomy, realistic expectations and suitable professional support.

lessons.title: Pain deserves attention
objectives: Choose stopping and assessment over enduring painful activity.
Prepare useful information for a clinician without self-diagnosing.
Recognise the limits of general courses and online remedies.
lessons.content:
Pain during sexual activity is a reason to pause or stop. You do not need to finish an activity, protect someone's feelings or prove that you can tolerate it. A partner's disappointment does not take priority over your comfort. You can say, “That hurts; I want to stop,” without first deciding what caused the pain.

Painful sex can have different causes, and assessment is needed to work out which care is appropriate. Jean Hailes advises seeing a doctor for painful sex; a clinician can investigate and arrange referral where needed. [B17] A description in an online lesson cannot distinguish among possible conditions. Do not assume pain is inevitable, purely psychological or a sign that someone is insufficiently interested. Equally, do not promise that a single product or technique will resolve it.

Prepare for an appointment by noting where discomfort occurs, when it started, how it feels, whether it happens outside sexual activity, and any other symptoms or relevant medicine changes. You may write this down instead of explaining everything aloud. Ask how an assessment will work, what your options are, and whether a relevant specialist referral would help. You can request a pause, explanation or support during care.

Avoid pushing through pain, using alcohol to ignore it, or copying exercises simply because they helped someone else. Different problems need different approaches. This course does not prescribe pelvic-floor exercises, numbing products, hormones or treatment. If symptoms are severe, sudden or worrying, seek urgent medical advice; Australia's healthdirect helpline can help assess the appropriate level of care. [B24]

While seeking support, intimacy can be redefined around what is genuinely comfortable and wanted. It may mean conversation, an agreed form of affection, time together without touch or taking space. Alternatives are invitations, not consolation tasks that must be accepted. A useful partner response is, “We can stop. What would help now?” The outcome to work toward is informed choice and wellbeing, not completion of a particular sexual act.

lessons.title: Desire, arousal and performance pressure
objectives: Separate bodily response from consent and personal worth.
Discuss different desire levels without creating a sexual obligation.
Identify when a persistent change warrants individual clinical advice.
lessons.content:
Sex is not an examination of worth, masculinity, femininity, attractiveness or relationship success. Bodies do not always respond on demand. Wanting affection, feeling desire, experiencing physical arousal and agreeing to an activity are related but different things. A physical response does not establish consent, and a lack of a particular response does not tell you the whole story of someone's feelings. [B11]

Healthdirect describes erectile difficulties as having possible physical and psychological contributors. It also explains that desire can change with stress, relationships, health conditions or medicines. Ongoing or distressing changes deserve an individual conversation with a qualified clinician. [B18, B19] Do not stop prescribed treatment, borrow a partner's medication or buy a promised cure on the strength of an advertisement. A useful question is, “This change is bothering me; what might be relevant, and what options can we discuss?”

Partners may want different amounts or kinds of sexual connection. A mismatch is information, not proof that one person is broken or failing the relationship. The person who wants more may feel disappointed; the person who wants less may feel pressured. Both feelings can be acknowledged while maintaining the same boundary: nobody owes sexual activity to regulate another person's emotions.

Choose a calm time to talk outside an immediate invitation. Describe your experience without assigning motives: “I miss feeling close” is more useful than “You never care about me.” Ask what forms of connection each person actually wants. Agreement is limited to the overlap, which may include no sexual activity. Scheduling time together is not a booking that must end in sex.

If a difference remains, people can consider individual support, relationship counselling when safe and mutually wanted, or decisions about compatibility. The aim is not to pressure the less interested person into meeting a quota. Curiosity and honest choices are better measures of progress than frequency, erection, orgasm or duration. Nobody needs to perform a body response to demonstrate learning in this course.

lessons.title: Distress, trauma-sensitive support and referral
objectives: Respond to distress without interpreting it as consent.
Offer support without demanding disclosure or taking control.
Distinguish education, therapy and urgent safety support.
lessons.content:
A sexual topic or interaction can bring up distress, memories or a feeling of disconnection. You do not need to explain why before asking to stop. During this course you can pause, use the text version, skip a reflection and return later. Learning about consent should leave you with more choice over the pace and amount of information you take in.

If someone becomes quiet, freezes, withdraws or seems unable to respond, stop the interaction and check what support they want. Do not assume a diagnosis from their behaviour, and do not treat the absence of resistance as agreement. Australian consent guidance explicitly warns that freezing and silence are not consent. [B11] Offer simple options such as space, a break or help contacting a trusted person; avoid unexpected touch or insisting they tell you what happened.

When someone discloses sexual violence, listen without blame. 1800RESPECT advises believing the person and recognising that there is no single correct way to respond to the experience. [B20] You can say, “Thank you for telling me. I am sorry this happened. What would help now?” They do not owe graphic details, a consistent emotional presentation or immediate decisions about reporting. Do not make promises of secrecy that you cannot keep; explain any actual limits to confidentiality in your role.

A partner or educator should not attempt trauma processing or insist on sexual activity as treatment. Suggest qualified support as an option, and let the person decide what help they want when possible. If fear, threats or coercion are present, prioritise safety support rather than negotiating access to sex. An apology or relationship label does not remove a person's right to distance.

In Australia, 1800RESPECT offers free information, counselling and support for people affected by domestic, family or sexual violence. [B22] For immediate danger or a medical emergency, call 000. This course can help you recognise a concern and find resources; it cannot assess an emergency, diagnose trauma or replace individual therapy. You can seek support without first deciding what label to give your experience.

modules.title: Putting learning into practice
modules.summary: Build a private plan, respond responsibly when something goes wrong, and know where to find trustworthy care and support.

lessons.title: Your private wellbeing and boundary plan
objectives: Turn learning into a small, realistic nonsexual action plan.
Separate boundaries, preferences and questions requiring advice.
Choose progress measures that do not reward sexual participation.
lessons.content:
A useful plan makes everyday decisions easier. It should not become a checklist of experiences you ought to have. Start with the life you want your choices to support: privacy, connection, independence, pleasure, health, rest or confidence. You can value several things at once. You can also decide that learning is enough for now and make no change to your sexual life.

Use four private headings: what matters to me; what I currently welcome or decline; what I want to understand better; and where I would seek help. Treat a preference as current information, not a prediction of your future. Treat a boundary as something others need to respect, not as a reason you must defend in detail. Relationships Australia WA offers guidance on identifying needs and communicating limits. [B23]

Choose one small action for the next month that does not require sexual activity. You might practise a sentence for saying no, check an app's privacy settings, bookmark a sexual health service, or learn the meaning of an unfamiliar term from a reputable source. If appropriate, prepare a question for a clinician. Keep the action small enough that missing it does not become another source of pressure.

Decide what information you want to record. You do not need a diary of sexual activity, partner names, fantasies or medical history to benefit from this course. A paper note you keep private may be enough; no upload is needed. Think about who can access any device or document before saving sensitive details. You can use a fictional plan instead of recording personal information.

Review progress through choices: Can I pause when unsure? Can I hear a no without punishing it? Do I know where to ask a health question? Can I distinguish a feeling from permission to act? Course completion shows engagement with learning tasks; it does not certify someone as a safe partner or authorise another person's consent. The plan belongs to you and can be changed, paused or discarded as your circumstances change.

lessons.title: Boundaries, repair and accountability
objectives: Distinguish a difference in preferences from a boundary violation.
Describe an accountable response without demanding forgiveness.
Recognise when safety support takes priority over a relationship discussion.
lessons.content:
Different preferences do not automatically mean someone has done something wrong. Two people may want different kinds of connection or have incompatible privacy expectations. The first task is to establish what each person actually wants. A respectful discussion can lead to a shared option, a pause or the decision that the relationship is not compatible. No one has to surrender a boundary to produce a tidy resolution.

When a boundary is crossed, focus on the action and its impact. Stop the behaviour. Check immediate needs without insisting on contact. Listen to the person's account without using your intentions as a defence. A useful acknowledgement names what you did: “I shared information you wanted private. I understand that was not mine to share.” Avoid apologies that shift responsibility, such as blaming the other person for not explaining perfectly.

Offer a concrete corrective step within your control and respect the answer. You might stop contacting someone, remove material you control, or seek independent help to change your own behaviour. Do not promise a result you cannot guarantee, such as deleting every copy someone else holds. An offer of repair is not a bargain for forgiveness, renewed access or reassurance. The affected person can decline further discussion.

Pressure or force around sexual activity is more serious than an ordinary disagreement. 1800RESPECT explains that a relationship does not give anyone the right to make another person do sexual things they do not want. [B21] If there are threats, fear or ongoing coercion, prioritise safety and specialist support. Do not require a joint conversation, mediation or an encounter with the person who caused harm.

For everyday disagreements, choose a calm time and a clear topic; speak about choices rather than character. For harm, accountability means changed conduct over time, with no entitlement to a second chance. You can learn to act differently while accepting that someone may want distance. The Academy's standard is respect for autonomy, including when the outcome is uncomfortable or the relationship ends.

objectives: Match a question to an appropriate type of support.

lessons.content:
Knowing where to ask is part of sexual wellbeing. A clinician can assess symptoms and discuss care. A peer service can offer understanding and help find options. A violence-support service can assist with safety and the effects of abuse. A regulator can explain reporting routes for online harm. These services have different roles; an influencer, course moderator or AI assistant cannot replace all of them.

lessons.title: Choosing touch and giving useful feedback
objectives: Describe a specific request without assuming a response.
Separate curiosity from an obligation to continue.
Use feedback that supports another person’s choices.
lessons.content:
A useful practical skill is describing an experience without turning it into a test. “Would you like a hug?” gives someone a choice. “You like hugs, don’t you?” can make disagreement harder. The same principle applies to sexual touch: name the proposed activity clearly enough to understand, leave room for refusal, and check again when something changes. Agreement to one kind of contact does not cover a different one. [R02]

Before any optional exploration, agree how to communicate pause, change and stop. People may prefer words, signs, writing or an agreed accessible signal. A stop signal is an additional tool, not the only way someone can withdraw. If a person becomes quiet, distressed or difficult to understand, pause and establish what they want rather than treating the absence of a signal as permission.

Useful feedback describes your own experience: “I prefer less pressure”, “Please stay with that”, “I would like a break”, or “I don’t want that today.” Receiving feedback means making the requested change without demanding a reason or taking it as a verdict on your worth. Thanking someone for speaking plainly can help make future conversations easier. These are suggested communication examples, not scripts that guarantee a particular result.

There is no required sequence from affection to genital contact to penetration. Partners can choose a single activity, return to something familiar, or spend time together without sex. A person can enjoy closeness while wanting no sexual contact. Curiosity about a topic in this course is also separate from wanting to try it.

After a conversation or an encounter, a brief optional check-in might ask what felt comfortable and what to approach differently next time. Do not make a partner rate your performance or reassure you before they can leave. Their feedback is useful information; their boundaries remain theirs to set. This lesson’s practice can be completed entirely with an everyday, nonsexual example.

lessons.title: Toys barriers and body care
objectives: Evaluate product information without relying on appearance or popularity.
Plan barrier and cleaning decisions before use.
Recognise when to stop and seek appropriate advice.
lessons.content:
A sexual product is an optional tool, not a requirement for satisfying intimacy. Start with its intended purpose, clear manufacturer instructions, dimensions, controls, power requirements, cleaning guidance and compatibility information. A recommendation on social media does not establish that a product suits your body or health circumstances. If instructions are unclear, seek reliable advice before use rather than improvising.

Read the instructions for the specific product and the barrier or lubricant being considered. Compatibility cannot be assumed from a colour, texture or the word “natural”. Use a new condom where required and do not reuse barriers. Healthdirect describes condoms as a way to reduce STI and pregnancy risk when used correctly; protection is not absolute. Follow the condom packet, including the lubricant guidance, and avoid using an internal and external condom together. [R10]

For shared products, agree on who will use them and the hygiene arrangements in advance. Follow the maker’s cleaning instructions and replace a condom when changing users or body sites. Never treat a quick wipe as proof that an item is ready for another person. Damage, cracks, unreliable controls or unclear suitability are reasons to set a product aside. These are practical consumer decisions rather than a guarantee that any material is universally safe.

For connected devices, discuss who can operate them, how control is disconnected and what account or usage information is recorded. Remote access requires ongoing agreement and a readily available way for the person using the device to stop it. A purchase or shared account does not authorise someone to activate it whenever they want.

Discomfort is useful information. Stop a product that causes pain, irritation or unwanted sensations. Seek medical advice for persistent pain, bleeding or an injury; do not use a course or product review to diagnose the cause. You can learn every concept in this lesson by evaluating a hypothetical instruction label, without buying or using a product.

lessons.title: Oral and genital contact
objectives: Discuss an activity using clear language rather than assumptions.
Recognise that oral contact can carry STI risk.
Prepare an activity-specific health conversation.
lessons.content:
Words such as “sex”, “foreplay” and “going further” can mean different things to different people. Naming the proposed activity helps someone understand what they are choosing. Oral contact means contact involving the mouth; genital contact can involve external touch or penetration. These categories describe activities, not a person’s orientation, experience or preferred role.

Ask about the contact someone wants, areas they want avoided and how they prefer to communicate changes. Agreement to kissing or external touch does not automatically include oral contact, penetration or contact with another body area. The right to stop applies throughout. Nobody needs to explain a boundary in enough detail to satisfy someone else. [R02]

Health planning should match the activity. STIs can be transmitted through oral, vaginal or anal contact, and some through skin contact in areas a barrier does not cover. Condoms and dams can reduce risk when used correctly; a lack of visible symptoms does not establish that an infection is absent. A sexual health professional can advise which tests and body sites are relevant to the contact you have had. [R09]

A useful conversation might ask: “What protection would help us feel comfortable?”, “Is there anything we should discuss before deciding?” and “What should we do if the barrier fails?” The conversation can happen before intimacy, when neither person feels rushed. You do not need to inspect another person’s medical records or demand a photograph of a test result as a condition of treating them respectfully.

Comfort also matters. Lubrication, pace, position and the choice to avoid penetration can be discussed without a performance target. If something hurts, pause or stop; recurring pain deserves assessment rather than pressure to push through. [R15] No activity in this lesson is a required milestone. Understanding the options and deciding against an activity are both valid learning outcomes.

objectives: Explain why anal contact needs its own agreement and preparation.
Identify basic evidence-based anal care principles.

If adults choose to discuss it, agree explicitly on the activity, boundaries, protection and stopping arrangements before anything begins. [R02]

The anus is the opening at the end of the bowel. Anal health information belongs in a clinical conversation that recognises sensitivity, comfort and infection risk. modules.title: Nonmonogamy and shared settings
modules.summary: Apply consent to relationship structures, multiple adults and changing agreements.

lessons.title: Agreements that include everyone
objectives: Distinguish a relationship agreement from control over another person.
Identify the people affected by a proposed change.
Plan a review conversation without demanding agreement.
lessons.content:
Monogamy, consensual nonmonogamy and being single are different ways adults may organise their relationships. None automatically tells you how respectfully the people involved behave. A label cannot replace an actual conversation about expectations, health, privacy, time and care.

An agreement is something the affected people understand and voluntarily accept. It should describe what each person is choosing rather than quietly assigning rights over someone who has not been consulted. For example, two established partners cannot agree between themselves that a new partner must share medical records, accept unequal treatment or be available on demand. The new person has their own choices.

Try discussing specific situations instead of a vague promise to “be open”. What counts as a date? What information should be shared, and when? Which details belong privately to another person? How will changes in sexual health plans be communicated? What happens if someone wants to pause their participation? The point is to make assumptions visible, not to produce a contract that cancels future consent. [R02]

Preferences can be incompatible. One person may want monogamy while another wants multiple relationships. It is possible to name that difference honestly without making either person prove they are enlightened, secure or loving enough. A respectful response might involve more discussion, remaining with existing mutually chosen arrangements, or deciding the relationship no longer fits. It does not require anyone to accept unwanted sexual situations.

Review conversations work best when people have time to consider a proposal and can say no without punishment. Do not announce a major change after acting on it and call the announcement consent. Also avoid promising confidentiality for another person’s intimate information when you intend to disclose it later.

These are ethical planning tools, not a guarantee that every disagreement will be solved. They help adults understand what is being requested and preserve each person’s ability to choose.

lessons.title: Invitations jealousy and group consent
objectives: Apply individual consent in a setting with several adults.
Respond to jealousy without using it as permission to control.
Plan a clear and independent exit option.
lessons.content:
Group settings create more communication tasks, not fewer rights. Agreement from one person does not speak for the rest of the group. An invitation, an event ticket or being present does not create permission to touch, photograph, watch or join an activity. Each proposed interaction needs the agreement of the relevant people. [R02]

Before attending a new setting, review its actual rules, privacy expectations, reporting route and ability to leave. A useful personal plan includes your own transport or another independent option, access requirements, a contact outside the setting if wanted and a sentence for declining. A reputation for being friendly is not a guarantee about every person present.

If someone changes their mind, stop involving them. Do not make the group vote on whether their reason is good enough. Other adults can decide separately what they want to do, but no one should pressure the person who has paused to remain, observe or reassure everyone. A host should make the reporting and exit route clear and respond to concerns without blaming the person who raises them.

Jealousy or uncertainty can be discussed as an experience: “I need time to understand this” or “This arrangement is not working for me.” The feeling is not proof that someone else has done wrong, and it does not justify surveillance, punishment or breaking another person’s privacy. Conversely, nobody has to dismiss their discomfort to prove that they are open-minded.

Make health and privacy discussions specific. Do not let the apparent confidence of a group substitute for your own understanding. Photographs require separate permission, including how they might be stored or shared. A later check-in can help identify what to change, but it cannot retrospectively authorise something that occurred without agreement.

lessons.title: Negotiating a first exploration
objectives: Separate a fantasy from an agreement to act.
Identify essential questions before an unfamiliar activity.
Recognise the limits of a written plan or stop word.
lessons.content:
A fantasy is an imagined possibility. It can be meaningful, enjoyable, confusing or something a person never wants to enact. Hearing about it is not permission to make it happen. Ask whether someone wants to discuss an idea, learn about it or consider a specific activity, and respect whichever answer they give.

For an unfamiliar activity, start with information rather than intensity. What exactly is being proposed? What does each person understand about its risks? What is outside scope? How will communication remain possible? What would make the plan stop? Are there health, access or emotional considerations the person chooses to mention? A lack of knowledge is a reason to seek reliable education or decline, not a challenge to prove courage.

Consent must remain voluntary throughout. [R02] An agreed role, a written plan or a stop word does not allow someone to ignore distress, uncertain communication or a withdrawal in ordinary language. Planning can improve clarity, but it does not turn a risky activity into a safe one or remove anyone’s responsibility to pay attention.

The Academy’s exploratory pathway focuses on communication, decision-making and lower-risk choices. It does not teach hazardous restraint, injury, breath restriction or medical procedures. If an activity requires specialist safety knowledge, this short course is not a qualification to perform it. People can explore a theme through discussion, fiction or a nonphysical role while choosing not to enact risk.

Agree on what support, distance or practical care each person may want afterward. Some people want conversation, some quiet and some to leave. Care is negotiated; it is not a debt. A follow-up message should also be welcome rather than assumed.

An appropriate outcome of negotiation can be “not now”, “not this activity” or “I do not want this”. Good negotiation creates clarity. It does not need to end with a yes.

objectives: Distinguish negotiated roles from entitlement.
Identify pressure disguised as expertise.
Choose support without requiring a confrontation.
lessons.content:
In a consensual role, adults may agree to a particular way of speaking, directing or responding. That agreement remains limited by what everyone actually wants. A role title, social reputation, teaching position or claim of experience is not authority over someone’s body, money, privacy or ability to leave.

Warning signs include refusing questions, treating limits as disobedience, insisting that beginners have no right to decide, threatening exclusion for declining and requiring secrecy about distress. A person does not need to establish someone else’s motives beyond doubt before deciding that a situation is unsuitable for them. Consent cannot be freely given when pressure and control remove a real choice. [R02]

Expertise should be open to scrutiny. A useful educator can explain their relevant qualifications, the limits of their knowledge and when another professional is needed. They should not promise that a particular practice is risk-free or use a student’s trust to seek sexual access. Learning about a practice is different from agreeing to do it with the teacher.

If something feels wrong, options include pausing, leaving, asking a trusted person for help, contacting an event organiser or using a specialist support service. You do not have to confront the person alone, educate them or persuade a group to agree before seeking support. If there is immediate danger, contact local emergency services.

Aftercare does not cancel a violation. An apology, gift or affectionate message cannot make a previous unwanted act consensual. Accountability involves respecting the person’s boundaries, avoiding retaliation and responding to the impact without demanding forgiveness.

A role title, social reputation, teaching position or claim of experience is not authority over someone’s body, money, privacy or ability to leave.

Warning signs include refusing questions, treating limits as disobedience, insisting that beginners have no right to decide, threatening exclusion for declining and requiring secrecy about distress. A person does not need to establish someone else’s motives beyond doubt before deciding that a situation is unsuitable for them. Consent cannot be freely given when pressure and control remove a real choice. [R02]

Expertise should be open to scrutiny. A useful educator can explain their relevant qualifications, the limits of their knowledge and when another professional is needed. They should not promise that a particular practice is risk-free or use a student’s trust to seek sexual access. Learning about a practice is different from agreeing to do it with the teacher.

If something feels wrong, options include pausing, leaving, asking a trusted person for help, contacting an event organiser or using a specialist support service. You do not have to confront the person alone, educate them or persuade a group to agree before seeking support. If there is immediate danger, contact local emergency services.

Aftercare does not cancel a violation. An apology, gift or affectionate message cannot make a previous unwanted act consensual. Accountability involves respecting the person’s boundaries, avoiding retaliation and responding to the impact without demanding forgiveness.

1800RESPECT provides support in Australia for people affected by domestic, family or sexual violence. [R14] The course can help identify options, but a learner decides what to disclose and which support to seek. Discussing a fictional case is enough to complete this lesson.

modules.title: Dating and digital choices
modules.summary: Make clear plans for meeting, privacy and online communication.

lessons.title: Planning a first meeting
objectives: Create a meeting plan that retains practical choices.
Distinguish online rapport from evidence of safety.
Recognise that accepting a date creates no sexual obligation.
lessons.content:
Online conversation can help people discover shared interests, but rapport is not verification of everything a person says. A thoughtful meeting plan gives you choices without requiring you to decide that the other person is definitely trustworthy or untrustworthy. You can want connection and still keep control over your time, information and ability to leave.

eSafety recommends considering privacy, warning signs and practical arrangements before meeting someone from an online service. Options include meeting in a public place, arranging your own transport and telling a trusted person your plan if that is safe for you. Avoid sharing home, workplace or other identifying details before you want to. No plan can guarantee safety or make someone responsible for another person’s abusive behaviour. [R12]

Discuss the type of meeting rather than relying on a suggestive joke. “I would like coffee and a conversation” is clear. If expectations differ, either person can decline. Buying a drink, travelling a long way or paying for a room never creates a sexual debt. Agreement to a date and agreement to sexual activity are separate. [R02]

Access needs deserve a place in the plan. Consider the venue’s accessibility, sensory environment, communication options, transport and support you choose. You may ask direct practical questions without sharing a diagnosis. A considerate response makes room for those questions rather than treating them as inconvenience.

If someone repeatedly ignores a boundary, pressures you to move off-platform or demands money or intimate content, pause and assess. You can end contact, use reporting or blocking tools and seek help. You do not owe continued conversation to prove that your concern is reasonable.

After a meeting, choose whether to remain in contact. A polite decline can be brief. Continued contact after a clear refusal is not persistence to admire. This exercise uses fictional plans; no actual meeting is required.

lessons.title: Sharing privacy without pressure
objectives: Distinguish consent to receive, create and share intimate content.
Recognise the limits of disappearing messages.
Identify a support route for non-consensual sharing.
lessons.content:
Digital intimacy has several separate decisions: whether to have a sexual conversation, receive an image, create content, store it and share it. Agreement to one does not cover the others. Ask before sending sexual content and respect a refusal without bargaining. A partner is allowed to enjoy a relationship without creating images. [R02]

If adults choose to share, discuss what is being agreed and the limits of technical controls. Disappearing messages and private accounts cannot guarantee that an image will not be copied, captured or retained elsewhere. Decide what identifying information you want to avoid and who has access to devices, backups and accounts. These considerations support choice; they do not make a person responsible if someone else violates that choice.

A request for deletion should be respected, while being honest that a sender may not be able to verify every copy. Avoid promises of perfect erasure. Recording a partner, uploading an intimate image to an AI system, changing its sexual context or sharing it with a group needs separate consideration and permission. Having received an image is not ownership of the person’s likeness.

eSafety describes image-based abuse as sharing, or threatening to share, intimate images or videos without consent and offers reporting and removal support. If blackmail is involved, do not send more money or intimate material. Seek support and preserve relevant information only where doing so is safe. [R13]

The Academy does not need intimate uploads for learning or assessment. Use fictional text examples when discussing digital choices. Keep identifying details out of a forum or help request unless a trusted service specifically needs them and explains why.

Respectful digital communication can be brief: “I’m not comfortable sending pictures” is a complete boundary. The other person’s disappointment does not turn it into a negotiation you must win.

modules.title: Intimacy through change and access
modules.summary: Adapt expectations and support autonomy when bodies, energy or circumstances change.

lessons.title: Changing bodies and expectations
objectives: Separate a change in sexual experience from personal failure.
Plan a conversation around present comfort and wishes.
Prepare an appropriate health question without self-diagnosing.
lessons.content:
Bodies and circumstances change. Ageing, pregnancy, recovery, illness, disability, stress, grief, medicines and gender-related care may prompt new questions about intimacy. The impact differs between people. The useful starting point is what this person is noticing and wants now, not a prediction based on their age, diagnosis or identity.

A previous pattern of sex does not become a duty during change. Ask what forms of closeness feel welcome, whether anything needs to pause and what practical support would help. Closeness can include conversation, affection, shared rest or no touch. It can also include sexual activity when everyone chooses it. None of these options needs to be treated as a lesser relationship.

If sex is painful or a change is persistent or concerning, a clinician can assess possible causes and discuss options. Pain can have different physical and psychological contributors; it should not be reduced to a character flaw or solved by pressure. [R15] Do not stop prescribed medicines or start a hormonal treatment because of a course example. Ask the prescribing clinician or another appropriate professional about individual concerns.

Prepare for an appointment by describing the symptom, when it occurs, its effect on daily life and the questions you want answered. You can ask for preferred language, a support person, an explanation before examination and time to decide. An educational worksheet is a memory aid, not a diagnostic test.

Changing expectations can involve loss as well as possibility. There is no requirement to feel positive immediately. A supportive conversation makes room for uncertainty and revisits plans without a deadline for returning to “normal”. A partner can express their own feelings without making someone else responsible for providing unwanted sex.

The goal is an approach that fits current wishes and circumstances. Success may mean more information, a useful referral, an honest boundary or a decision to wait.

lessons.title: Supporting access together
objectives: Ask about access without taking over another adult’s decisions.
Design more than one communication route.
Identify when support roles create pressure or conflicts.
lessons.content:
Accessibility begins with the person’s preferences. Ask what would make a conversation, venue or learning task work for them. Do not assume that a disability, support need or communication difference reveals whether someone wants sex, can make decisions or needs another person to speak for them.

Build communication around the methods the person uses. That may include speech, text, signs, AAC, extra processing time or a clear yes/no format. Check understanding without interrogating or infantilising. If you cannot establish agreement through a reliable shared method, pause. Respecting autonomy includes providing the conditions for an informed, voluntary choice. [R02]

Practical changes can be simple: a quieter room, breaks, less visual stimulation, a different time of day, an accessible venue or a plan that does not involve touch. Ask before moving a mobility aid, touching a body part or involving a support person. A person may welcome help with logistics while wanting privacy about relationships.

Support roles can create unequal power. Housing, personal care, employment or access to communication should never be made conditional on sexual participation. An adult who relies on another person for assistance still has boundaries. If a support arrangement feels coercive or unsafe, specialist support can help explore options without requiring the person to solve it alone. [R14]

For partners, sharing effort means agreeing on what is useful rather than treating one person as a project. For educators, access means offering equivalent ways to demonstrate learning. A learner may use the fictional scenario, answer in text, take more time or skip private reflection and still work toward the same knowledge outcome.

There is no universal accessible sex script. The repeatable skill is asking, listening, adapting and checking again. The person’s answer can change, and the plan should leave space for that.

capstone.title: Making informed choices
capstone.instructions: Allow approximately 15 minutes for the 12 capstone questions, 20 minutes for the fictional planning task and its six applied decisions, and five minutes for feedback. There is no enforced time limit. Score at least 10 of 12 on the capstone and resolve every safety-critical item. All six applied-case decisions must also be correct, or a human reviewer must confirm all six criteria in the written alternative. No personal disclosure or sexual activity is required.
capstone.planningPassRule: All six applied-case decisions correct after feedback; alternatively, all six written rubric criteria met following human review.

sources.title: Emergency contraception: an overview
supports: Starting hormonal contraception immediately after ulipristal may reduce the effectiveness of emergency and ongoing contraception; a five-day delay is advised.
Condoms or abstaining from pregnancy-risk sex are needed during that delay and until the regular method becomes effective, with timing dependent on the method.
A dose of oral emergency contraception does not provide ongoing protection from later sex.
Follow-up pregnancy testing may be indicated.
